content: In certain cases, friendly competitions or national ranking systems have proven effective, as demonstrated in Madagascar's case study. Alternatively, facilities may receive financial or non-financial rewards for achieving specific targets or standards. However, it is crucial to address potential biases among groups responsible for inspecting and regulating these facilities. Engaging users and communities to review and provide feedback on water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services can be a valuable method to validate data. In Liberia, the 2014–2016 Ebola outbreak, which claimed 4,810 lives, highlighted the severe limitations of WASH services and infection prevention and control (IPC) in healthcare facilities. As part of the recovery process, the health system recognized the need for minimum WASH standards. In 2016, Liberia's Vice President launched a minimum WASH package, including new standards and the adoption of WASH FIT as the national implementation tool. District health teams, in collaboration with a national WASH FIT team, assumed responsibility for regular supervision and mentoring. This initiative prioritized WASH in quality and health security efforts, embedded it into national strategies, and catalyzed the development of broader WASH standards, including those for drinking water quality and healthcare waste. However, challenges such as limited governance and insufficient funding hinder frequent supervision visits. The establishment of a National WASH Commission with a dedicated budget aims to address these issues. In Tajikistan, the introduction of WASH FIT in 2018 helped set specific targets for WASH in healthcare facilities, aligning with WHO and UNECE protocols. The Ministry of Health and Social Protection took the lead in integrating WASH requirements into policies and standards, fostering collaboration with partners like Oxfam. Despite outdated infrastructure requiring significant investment, WASH FIT has enabled facilities to prioritize improvements and achieve progress with limited resources. In Sierra Leone, the Ministry of Health and Sanitation addressed healthcare waste management issues exacerbated during the Ebola epidemic. By modifying the design of De Montfort incinerators using locally available materials, the country developed context-specific solutions validated against performance standards. These efforts included training healthcare waste technicians and creating national standards for rural primary healthcare centers. However, challenges such as understaffing and high turnover among healthcare workers persist, emphasizing the need for proper waste segregation and sustained investment in waste treatment systems. In Nepal, bio-digesters were introduced to manage infectious organic waste in healthcare facilities. For example, Bir Hospital in Kathmandu installed a bio-digester in 2011 to treat food and maternity waste. Locally designed systems treat up to 220 kg of waste daily, producing biogas for facility kitchens. While energy production is a modest co-benefit, the primary goal remains safe waste management. Replication of this model in other regions, such as Tanzania and Madagascar, highlights its potential. However, proper training and ongoing monitoring are essential for successful implementation. In Madagascar, the government adapted a three-star approach, initially used in schools, to improve WASH in healthcare facilities. Starting in 2014, this program encouraged facilities to make incremental improvements in hygiene practices and infrastructure, aiming to meet national standards. By 2018, the program reached 590 rural healthcare facilities, representing 20% of the country's rural primary healthcare centers. This initiative equipped healthcare personnel with tools and training to adopt hygienic practices, improve patient satisfaction, and promote safer waste disposal methods. Alcohol-based hand rub (ABHR) has been recognized as a lifesaving technology, particularly in resource-limited settings. WHO has provided a formula and implementation guide for local production since 2009, and ABHR was added to the WHO List of Essential Medicines in 2015. While ABHR improves hand hygiene where resources like sinks, water, and soap are unavailable, it is not a substitute for safe, reliable water supplies. Efforts to secure water for drinking, cleaning, and hygiene must continue alongside ABHR availability. In Uganda, the Ministry of Health integrated WASH indicators into the national health management information system (HMIS) in 2016. This effort, supported by partners, aimed to collect reliable WASH data for planning and budgeting. Uganda is among the few countries to incorporate WASH indicators into a digital platform, enabling better analysis and harmonization with global monitoring systems. In Lao PDR, a 2014 assessment revealed significant gaps in WASH services in healthcare facilities. In response, the National Centre for Environmental Health and Water Supply developed a national policy on WASH and healthcare waste management. The WASH FIT tool was introduced in 2018 to translate these policies into actionable improvements at the facility level. In Tanzania, the Soapbox Collaborative developed the TEACH CLEAN training package to address inadequate training and supervision of hospital cleaners. This participatory program, adapted by Tanzania's national training institute in 2018, aims to improve cleaning behavior and hygiene levels in healthcare facilities. Initial assessments and evaluations are underway to inform broader implementation in other contexts.
